title: Antony's laughter (Life of Antony)
hookLine: Athanasius shows Antony laughing at the demons' threats
tomorrow: what do you put on before you walk out the door?

cards: Fear gets loud at three in the morning. Every creak becomes a burglar, every worry a disaster.
A man named Antony shut himself in an old tomb to pray, and one night, the story says, the walls seemed to split and fill with roaring: lions, bears, leopards, bulls, serpents, scorpions, wolves.
Bruised, lying on the floor, he answered them. He mocked them.

teach.h: IF YOU HAD POWER, ONE WOULD DO.
teach.b: The question is old: what do you do with a fear that roars? Here's the answer in the Life of Antony, told by Athanasius, a bishop who knew him. First, the mockery.
In pain but clear-headed, Antony tells the shapes: if you had any real power, one of you would be enough. You come as a crowd, wearing the shapes of beasts, because you're weak.
Second, the light. A ray breaks through the roof, the shapes vanish, the pain stops. Where were you, Antony asks.
A voice answers that it was there all along, watching him fight. Third, the teaching.
Later Antony tells the monks the demons are noisy but powerless, and what they want most is your fear. Fourth, a neighbor. Buddhists tell stories with the same nerve.
In the Samyutta Nikaya, a collection of the Buddha's discourses, Mara the tempter comes to the Buddha in frightening shapes, once as a huge elephant, once as a giant serpent.
Each time the Buddha simply recognizes him: this is Mara.
And Mara, knowing he's been seen, vanishes. Both say a terror loses its grip once it's seen for what it is. The honest difference: Antony's courage rests on the Lord who was there all along.
In the Buddha's story no voice comes from above; the clear seeing is itself the freedom.

how: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Antony of the desert each year, and the Life of Antony is still read in monasteries and by people learning to pray.

o: refusing to be impressed by a fear that roars
a joke told at a funeral to ease the grief
the sound a monk makes when he breaks his silence

p: there all along, watching him fight

s: Antony laughed because he wasn't really hurt or afraid of anything
Athanasius says he was in pain; his mind was clear, and he refused to be impressed.
in the story, a light breaks through the roof and the shapes vanish
then a voice tells him it was there all along.
in the Buddhist stories, the Buddha drives Mara off by fighting him
he recognizes Mara, and Mara, knowing he's been seen, vanishes.

games.q: your little brother can't sleep after a scary video. it's all he talks about. what would Antony's way look like?
o: say the fear out loud together, and notice how weak it sounds.
tell him fears aren't real, so he should stop thinking about it.
leave every light on all week until he forgets the video.
games.why: Antony named the shapes' weakness out loud: if you had power, one would be enough. his laughter wasn't denial; it was refusing to be impressed.

practice: On a scrap of paper, write one small fear, the kind that roars more than it bites, in plain words. Read it back slowly and notice how it sounds when it isn't growling; if a smile comes, let it.
A bigger fear, one that feels dangerous or won't let you sleep, deserves a real person: in danger in the US, call or text 988, or your local emergency number.

wordCard.voice: Antony's laughter. A man in a dark tomb who hears all the roaring and isn't impressed.

orig.note: Greek for laughter, the language Athanasius wrote the Life of Antony in.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: laughing at demons, a crowd of shapes without one real power among them. Rest well tonight.
